rows.title: Power Steering Pump / System Leak & Whine — Reservoir Screen Clog and Seal Failure

rows.title: Catalytic Converter Efficiency Below Threshold (P0420 / P0430) — Aging or Manifold-Integrated Cats
rows.howToFix: Diagnose before buying a cat: scan for misfire codes (P030x/P0300), check for exhaust leaks upstream, and compare upstream vs downstream O2/A-F sensor waveforms. If sensors and exhaust are healthy and the downstream signal tracks the upstream, replace the failed converter. On 4th-gen 4.0L trucks the failure is usually the passenger-side (Bank 1) manifold-integrated cat. Use OEM or a high-quality CARB-compliant converter; a common contributing fix is the Bank 1 Sensor 2 (downstream) O2 sensor (use Denso). Sensor-only fixes run $100-300; converter replacement is the expensive path.

rows.title: 1ZZ-FE Engine Excessive Oil Consumption (GT)
rows.howToFix: Confirm excessive consumption by performing an oil consumption test after ruling out external leaks from the valve cover, timing chain tensioner, and oil pan, then check compression/leak-down and inspect spark plugs and the catalytic converter for oil fouling. The permanent repair is an engine teardown with updated Toyota pistons and oil-control rings/ring set (many shops replace all four pistons/rings and rod bearings while the engine is apart), along with cylinder honing, new gaskets/seals, and often a timing chain set if wear is present. If oil burning has already contaminated the exhaust, the upstream O2 sensor and catalytic converter may also need replacement. Typical cost is about $2,500-$4,500 for a piston/ring rebuild, while a used or remanufactured replacement engine can run roughly $3,000-$6,000 installed.

rows.title: 2ZZ-GE Lift Bolt Failure (GT-S)

Parts are usually inexpensive (roughly $20-$60 for bolts, gasket, and related small parts), while total repair cost is commonly about $250-$600 depending on labor and whether additional valvetrain damage or oiling issues are found.

Toyota's TSB specifies a special procedure when using AC Power Foam Evaporator Cleaner on these models. Run the AC on recirculate for 10 minutes with windows open periodically to dry the evaporator. For persistent odor, the evaporator may need cleaning with Toyota-approved AC cleaner. Preventive tip: run the fan on high with AC off for 5 minutes before parking to dry the evaporator.

rows.title: Milky/Discolored Engine Oil from Condensation
rows.howToFix: This is primarily a driving pattern issue. Take the vehicle on longer drives (20+ minutes at highway speed) at least once a week to allow the engine to reach full operating temperature and burn off moisture. If oil appears milky, change it promptly. Toyota's TSB recommends following the shorter oil change interval (5,000 miles) if the vehicle is primarily used for short trips. Do not confuse this with head gasket failure — the M20A engine does not have widespread head gasket issues.

rows.title: Hybrid System Software Glitches and Hesitation

Some owners report that Sport mode provides more consistent power delivery. The issue improves with newer software versions.

If the noise persists, inspect the front strut mounts for looseness or bearing failure. Toyota has released updated end links with improved bushings for 2024+ production. rows.howToFix: Replace both the clutch master cylinder and slave cylinder together — they typically fail in quick succession. Since the slave cylinder requires transmission removal, replace the clutch disc and pressure plate at the same time (even if they have life remaining) to avoid paying for transmission removal again. Use a Toyota OEM slave cylinder as aftermarket units have a high failure rate.

rows.howToFix: Replace the valve cover gasket with a Toyota OEM gasket kit that includes spark plug tube seals. Clean all oil residue from the exhaust manifold after replacing. Replace the oil filler cap O-ring (or the entire cap for $10). Apply a thin bead of RTV sealant only at the cam cap corners where the valve cover gasket doesn't seal perfectly.

rows.title: Power Steering Rack Seal Leak
rows.howToFix: Replace the power steering rack assembly. Aftermarket remanufactured racks are available for $200-$350. Flush the entire power steering system with new fluid after installation. A temporary fix is to use a power steering stop-leak additive, but this only works for minor seeps. Check for contaminated fluid (dark or burnt smell) indicating internal pump damage.

rows.title: Rear Brake Drum Seizure and Self-Adjuster Failure
rows.howToFix: Remove rear drums (may require penetrating oil and a hammer), clean all components, replace shoes if glazed or contaminated. Free up and lubricate the self-adjuster mechanism with high-temp brake grease. Replace the parking brake cable if seized. Apply anti-seize compound to the drum-to-hub contact surface. Exercise the parking brake regularly to prevent recurrence.

rows.title: Rear Wheel Bearing Premature Failure
rows.howToFix: Replace the failed rear wheel bearing. The bearings are pressed into the hub assembly and require a hydraulic press for removal and installation. Replace both sides if one has failed — the other typically follows within 10,000-20,000 miles. Some owners replace the entire hub/knuckle assembly from a junkyard as it can be faster and cheaper than pressing bearings.

rows.title: Front Suspension Knock from Strut Top Mounts
rows.howToFix: Replace the front strut top mounts and bump-stop/dust-boot kits on both sides; check stabilizer-bar end links and bushings and the lower ball joints while the suspension is apart. If the struts themselves are worn or were damaged by the loose mounts, replace them in pairs. On cars within warranty, Toyota dealers have replaced struts and mount kits under warranty — document the noise and insist on the inspection. The noise commonly returns if only the bump stop is replaced and the top mount is left in place.

Cars still in the 3-year warranty window should insist on warranty coverage — Toyota repaired several publicized cases free of charge. On 2017+ cars with a soft/sinking pedal, inspect the hydraulic actuator and lines for leaks and replace the actuator, bleeding the system and replacing contaminated fluid.

rows.title: Water and Dust Infiltration into Cabin and Trunk
rows.howToFix: Identify the entry point: common culprits are deteriorated or displaced door and trunk-lid weatherstrips, the trunk-lid latch sitting too high to compress the seal, dirty/failed seam sealant around the tail-light housings, and door membrane/vent sealing. Fixes that worked for owners include adjusting the trunk latch so the lid compresses the rubber seal, removing the tail lights and re-applying sealant, replacing weatherstrips, and resealing door vapor barriers. Dry the carpet and underlay completely to avoid mold and corrosion. Persistent cases under warranty should be escalated with photos, as multiple visits are often needed.

The lasting fix is a proper repaint of affected panels (roof, pillars, gutters) by a quality body shop with correct primer prep — dealer respray quality varies and recurrences are documented. rows.title: Infotainment Software Bugs and Display Issues
rows.howToFix: First verify the concern by checking the multimedia head unit for stored diagnostic trouble codes and confirming the current software/calibration version with Toyota Techstream or the vehicle’s built-in update menu. If blackouts or audio loss continue after updates, inspect the head unit connectors, USB hub, and battery voltage/ground integrity, and replace the display/audio head unit only if Toyota diagnostics confirm hardware failure; software updates are often free under warranty, while out-of-warranty diagnosis typically runs about $150-$250 and head unit replacement can exceed $1,200-$2,500.

If sludge is present, remove the oil pan and valve covers to physically clean the pickup screen and galleries; severe cases with spun bearings or scored cams require a rebuilt/replacement engine. rows.title: 3-Speed Transmission: Tall Gearing & Brittle Case
rows.howToFix: The classic, well-documented upgrade is the H42 4-speed swap. The 1975–79 (10/73–7/80) H42 4-speed bolts up to the earlier transfer case, giving a proper road gear plus better ratios. The job needs a 4-speed bellhousing, the correct transmission output gear, an output bearing, and the 4-speed shift linkage/front-output shift fork — kits (e.g. CruiserParts' 3-to-4-speed conversion) bundle the parts. Builders deliberately choose the EARLY H42 (pre-8/80) because the later 19-spline output and bolt pattern won't mate to the one-piece transfer case. If keeping the 3-speed, restorers at minimum rebuild it with fresh synchros and handle the brittle case carefully.

rows.title: FJ40 Body Tub & Quarter-Panel Rust (Rockers, Floors, Wheel Arches, Cowl)
rows.howToFix: Restorers cut out ALL the rot rather than coat over it, then weld in reproduction steel: CCOT/Specter/Aqualu 16-gauge quarter-panel patch panels and dogleg sections, new rocker/sill panels, and full replacement or fabricated floor pans (many builds upgrade to heavier diamond-plate floors). Critically, the proven bulletproofing step is to treat the inside of the boxed cavities AFTER welding — flush with rust converter/epoxy primer and pump cavity wax (Cosmoline/Fluid Film/Eastwood) into the rockers, quarters and frame rails so the repair doesn't simply rot again from within. Epoxy-prime bare steel immediately, seam-seal all overlaps, and undercoat. Frame rot is addressed by boxing/plating the rails or, in severe cases, a replacement frame.

rows.title: Front Axle Knuckle / Birfield & Trunnion Bearing Wear
rows.howToFix: The proven fix is a full front-axle knuckle overhaul: disassemble the knuckles, replace all four Koyo trunnion/knuckle bearings and races as a set (they wear evenly, so do them together), re-shim the king-pin preload to spec, and install a complete knuckle rebuild kit (inner axle seals, felt wipers, gaskets, lock washers). A clever bulletproofing trick veterans use is to SWAP the birfields side-to-side so the worn face is unloaded, extending their life, and to repack with proper moly birfield grease. For hard use, heavy-duty (Marlin Crawler) inner seals keep contamination out so the rebuild lasts.

rows.title: Inadequate Drum Brakes (Single-Circuit Early Cars)
rows.howToFix: The standard restoration upgrade is a front (or full four-wheel) disc-brake conversion. Well-proven kits from JTOutfitters, Cruiser Corps, Manafre and Specter swap the front drums for discs, and rear kits commonly adapt affordable mid-'80s GM Monte Carlo calipers. Pair the discs with the correct later-model brake booster (the trick is grabbing the complete later pedal box so the booster bolts up) and, on early trucks, convert the single-circuit system to a DUAL-circuit master cylinder with re-plumbed lines so a single failure can't kill all braking. Finish with stainless flex lines and a fresh proportioning valve for balanced, fade-resistant stopping.

rows.title: Sloppy Recirculating-Ball Steering Box & Worn Linkage
rows.howToFix: The right restoration approach is to renew the whole steering chain, not just chase the box: replace all tie-rod and relay-rod ends, the steering U-joints, and the spring bushings first, then rebuild or replace the steering box with a fresh seal kit and CORRECTLY shimmed on-center lash (snug at center, not bound). Many restorers upgrade to a later FJ40 factory power-steering box (1979–84) for far better feel, or fit a modern EZ Electric Power Steering kit (Koyo/NSK components) that bolts to the column for effortless, precise steering. A correctly set, rebuilt box plus tight linkage transforms the drive.

rows.title: Undersized Cooling System — F/2F Overheating
rows.howToFix: The community bulletproofing recipe: fit a high-capacity aftermarket aluminum radiator (3- or 4-core, often a CSF or Wizard Cooling unit), add a proper full radiator SHROUD (the single biggest free improvement to airflow), and replace the old flex fan with a quality fan clutch or a high-flow electric fan setup. Run a new high-flow water pump and a correct-temp thermostat with a fresh O-ring/seal, then back-flush or rod-out the block water jackets if the truck sat. Always bleed the system fully on refill. Many restorers also delete chronic air pockets with a proper fill/bleed procedure and keep a 50/50 coolant mix with a quality cap that holds rated pressure.

rows.title: Weak Charging & Aging Electrical System
rows.howToFix: Restorers convert to a modern internally-regulated alternator — either an upgraded Toyota internal-regulator unit (e.g. the 55A 27020-61071 family) or a higher-output GM Delco (CS130, up to ~105A) on a bracket adapter. The key bulletproofing detail the forums stress: run the high-output alternator's main charge wire DIRECTLY to the battery with appropriately sized cable rather than back through the stock harness, and wire the alternator's sense terminal to the fuse block so it compensates for voltage drop (brighter lights, better charge). Refresh grounds, replace crusty bullet connectors, and on 6-volt trucks do a full 12-volt conversion. A new reproduction harness is the gold-standard fix for a brittle original.

rows.title: Body and frame rust: rear quarter panels, rockers, and frame rails
rows.howToFix: Cut out and weld in replacement quarter-panel/rocker repair sections (reproduction doglegs and OEM-style panels are available), fix the water-intrusion source (reseal windows and tailgate), and treat/cavity-wax the frame. For surface frame rust, media-blast and coat; for perforated frame or body mounts, weld in new steel. Preventive rinsing of the rear arches and undercoating markedly slows progression.

rows.title: Front axle knuckle service neglect / birfield wear and knuckle seal leaks

Swapping birfields side-to-side extends their life since they wear on one side. Address a warped housing if seals wear abnormally fast, and use the correct-era birfields when replacing. Many owners DIY this; a shop rebuild of both sides is straightforward but labor-intensive.

rows.title: Center Differential Lock Actuator Failure

In some cases, the transfer case shift fork is worn and requires transfer case disassembly ($800-$1,500 labor). Test the center diff lock regularly (monthly) to keep the mechanism exercised — Land Cruisers that never use the diff lock are more prone to actuator seizure.

If ceramic debris has already been ingested and compression is poor or oil consumption remains high, the engine may require teardown or replacement short block, which can raise total repair cost into the $3,000-$6,000 range.

rows.title: Clutch Cable Breakage

Also inspect the pedal bracket and firewall for cracking or misalignment that can accelerate cable wear. Parts typically cost about $30-$90, and replacement usually takes 1-2 hours, for a total repair cost of roughly $120-$300 at a shop.

rows.title: Frame Rust and Structural Corrosion
rows.howToFix: Inspect the entire frame with the truck on a lift, paying close attention to the inside and lower surfaces of the boxed rails, rear spring hangers, steering box area, crossmembers, and body mounts; use a hammer or pick test to identify soft spots, perforation, and delamination hidden under scale. If corrosion is limited to surface rust, mechanically remove scale, treat with rust converter, then apply epoxy chassis coating and internal frame cavity wax, typically costing about $500-$1,500. If there is perforation, cracked mounts, or significant thinning, the only proper repair is sectioning in heavy-gauge frame repair plates by a qualified welder/fabricator or replacing the frame entirely with a rust-free southern/western donor, with repairs commonly running $2,000-$6,000+ and severely rusted trucks often being uneconomical to save. After repair, recheck alignment and suspension mounting points, and perform annual rustproofing to slow recurrence.

If the bulletin's rear differential failure-mode data are confirmed, Toyota directs rear differential carrier replacement and 4WD ECU reprogramming; a confirmed front-transfer failure follows a different path. The original Toyota powertrain coverage was 60 months/60,000 miles from first use and will generally be expired; confirm any current coverage before authorizing work. Coverage is offered for ten years from the vehicle's date of first use regardless of mileage, subject to program terms and a verified covered leak. The dealer confirms the source, selects revised clips, pads, retainers and seals for the installed roof-rail configuration, performs a shower test, and cleans, repairs or replaces covered water-damaged components through the program process. Do not buy the removed campaign-part searches or simply dry the headliner before the leak source and coverage are established.

rows.title: Secondary Air Injection System Failure (2UZ-FE)
rows.howToFix: Replace air switching valves (Toyota 25701-50040 and 25702-50011) and air injection pump (Toyota 17610-0S010) if seized. Many owners bypass the system entirely with block-off plates since it only operates during cold start for emissions. Bypass plates available from Trail Gear or fabricated from aluminum.

rows.title: Exhaust Manifold Cracking (4.7L 2UZ-FE V8)
rows.howToFix: Replace the cracked exhaust manifold ($300-$600 per side for parts). Both sides should be inspected as cracking often affects both manifolds. The exhaust manifold studs frequently break during removal due to corrosion — budget for stud extraction or replacement ($100-$200 extra). Total repair with gaskets and hardware runs $800-$1,500 per side at a shop. Aftermarket stainless steel headers ($400-$800 per side) are a popular upgrade that resists cracking. Always replace the manifold gaskets during the repair.

rows.title: Frame Rust and Structural Corrosion
rows.howToFix: For surface rust: wire brush, treat with POR-15 or Eastwood Rust Encapsulator, and apply Fluid Film annually. For structural rust: professional frame repair with welded reinforcement plates or boxed sections. Severe cases may require frame replacement from a southern/western donor vehicle. Annual undercoating with Fluid Film or Woolwax is essential for prevention.
rows.dispositionReason: At least one replacement is conditional on a stated diagnostic result.

rows.title: Rear Liftgate Strut Failure (Hatch Won't Stay Open)
rows.howToFix: Replace both rear liftgate struts at the same time — they are sold in pairs for $30-$80. Installation takes 10-15 minutes with no tools required on most models (the struts pop on and off ball studs). OEM Toyota struts are available for $40-$60 each, and aftermarket options from Stabilus, StrongArm, or Sachs run $15-$30 each. Always replace both struts even if only one has failed — if one is weak, the other is close behind. This is one of the easiest DIY repairs on the Sequoia.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

For towing overheating: ensure the transmission cooler and auxiliary cooler (if equipped with tow package) are functioning. Toyota has issued TSBs addressing cooling system software calibration. Verify all cooling system software is at the latest version.

Labor is significant due to door panel and inner mechanism access.

rows.title: Power Steering Rack Seal Leak

A new OEM rack is $600-$1,200. As a temporary measure, topping off the power steering fluid and adding a stop-leak additive (Lucas Power Steering Stop Leak, $10) can slow a minor leak for several months. A four-wheel alignment ($100-$150) is required after rack replacement. The 2021+ Sienna uses electric power steering and does not have this issue.

The hybrid battery is covered under Toyota 10-year/150,000-mile hybrid component warranty. Keep the battery cooling fan intake (under the rear seat) clean and unobstructed — poor airflow is the leading cause of premature hybrid battery degradation.

Use genuine Toyota hydraulic fluid (not generic ATF) to prevent seal damage. For stuck tops, check the hydraulic fluid level first — a simple top-off may restore function temporarily. If hydraulic cylinders leak, rebuild or replace them ($300-$600 each). Check the convertible top control module for water damage. Flush and replace hydraulic fluid every 5 years as preventive maintenance.

rows.title: Dashboard Melting and Becoming Sticky
rows.howToFix: Contact Toyota dealer to check for extended warranty coverage (Customer Support Program ZE7). If covered, Toyota will replace the dashboard at no cost. rows.title: Frame Rust and Corrosion

rows.title: Automatic Transmission Failure (A132L)
rows.howToFix: Start by confirming the failure with a road test and transmission line-pressure/scan diagnosis, then inspect fluid condition, pan debris, shift solenoids, and the valve body for sticking valves or worn bores. Typical costs are about $300-$700 for diagnostic work and minor valve body/fluid repairs, $1,800-$3,000 for a proper rebuild, or $800-$1,500 for a used replacement transmission plus installation; because used units are often worn, many owners instead swap to a manual gearbox when economically practical.

rows.title: Starter Motor Failure (Buried Under Intake Manifold)
rows.howToFix: Confirm the starter (voltage at the solenoid, bench test) before tearing in. Replace the starter motor — often with a Denso OEM or quality reman unit — while the intake is off; many owners also refresh the intake gaskets and PCV components at the same time to avoid repeating the labor. Budget roughly 4-5 hours labor due to intake removal.

rows.title: VVT-i Intake Cam Gear Cold-Start Rattle
rows.howToFix: If the rattle is brief and oil pressure is good, switching to a quality full-synthetic oil with strong cold-flow and anti-drainback behavior (and shorter change intervals) often reduces or eliminates it. Persistent or loud rattle warrants inspection per the applicable Toyota TSB and replacement of the intake-side VVT cam gear/actuator. Keep oil level correct and use the specified 0W-20/5W-20 to maintain VVT response.

rows.title: Water Pump Bearing and Seal Failure
rows.howToFix: Replace the water pump along with thermostat, coolant, and serpentine belt as preventive maintenance. OEM water pump replacement costs $400-$800 including labor.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Denso Low-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure and Stalling (Recall)
rows.howToFix: Covered under Toyota recall / Customer Support Program — dealer replaces the low-pressure fuel pump with an improved-impeller design at no charge. Verify the VIN on the NHTSA or Toyota recall site. Out-of-coverage replacement involves dropping or accessing the in-tank pump assembly. Reimbursement may be available for prior out-of-pocket repairs.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Verify the VIN on the NHTSA or Toyota recall site.

rows.dispositionReason: The prescribed remedy is dealer, campaign, recall, or software work.

rows.title: Backup Camera Blank/Green Screen on 14-inch Display (Recall)
rows.howToFix: Covered by recall — dealer installs a multimedia software update at no cost; reimbursement available for prior related repairs. Check the VIN on the NHTSA or Toyota recall portal. As an interim measure a multimedia reboot (long-press power) may temporarily restore the screen, but the software update is the fix.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Check the VIN on the NHTSA or Toyota recall portal.

rows.dispositionReason: The prescribed remedy is dealer, campaign, recall, or software work.

rows.title: Multimedia/Infotainment System Freezing, Rebooting, and PIN Loop
rows.howToFix: First-line fix: in the Toyota app, delete the vehicle from the profile (or log out, change password/PIN, log back in) then re-link the truck via the in-dash QR code — this clears the PIN loop. A multimedia reboot (press-and-hold the power/volume knob ~10-20 seconds) clears most freezes. Dealers can apply multimedia software updates that address several of these bugs; ensure the unit is on the latest version.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Panoramic Moonroof Spontaneous Shattering
rows.howToFix: Document the failure (photos, note absence of impact) and file an NHTSA complaint; pursue warranty/goodwill, as outcomes vary. Repair requires replacing the moonroof glass and clearing all shattered fragments from the headliner and tracks; budget for headliner R&R. Aftermarket glass is available but OEM fit is recommended for the panoramic assembly.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Rear Load-Leveling Air Suspension Bottoming Out / Harsh Ride
rows.howToFix: Have the dealer verify the air suspension is leveling correctly and check for stored height-control faults and any applicable software calibration updates. Confirm correct ride height and that no leveling kit is interfering with the sensors. Some owners improve ride by addressing tire/wheel choice (E-rated tires on 20-inch wheels ride harder). Replace failed air struts/compressor/height sensors if a component fault is found.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Have the dealer verify the air suspension is leveling correctly and check for stored height-control faults and any applicable software calibration updates.
Confirm correct ride height and that no leveling kit is interfering with the sensors.

rows.title: Turbocharger Electronic Wastegate Actuator Failure (V35A Twin-Turbo)
rows.howToFix: Scan for boost-control/wastegate codes and confirm actuator function. Under powertrain warranty Toyota replaces the affected turbocharger/wastegate assembly. For the early-2022 'bad batch,' replacement of the updated actuator/turbo resolves the recurring CEL. Out of warranty this is a major repair; some independent shops can replace just the actuator on the updated procedure where supported.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Scan for boost-control/wastegate codes and confirm actuator function.

rows.title: Twin-Turbo V6 Engine Bearing Failure
rows.howToFix: Toyota will inspect and replace affected engines under recall free of charge. Engine replacement is the primary remedy. Owners experiencing symptoms should stop driving immediately and contact Toyota.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Toyota will inspect and replace affected engines under recall free of charge.

rows.title: 2AR-FE Engine Excessive Oil Consumption
rows.howToFix: Request Toyota oil consumption test at dealer. If consumption exceeds 1 qt per 1,200 miles, piston and ring replacement is covered under warranty enhancement ZE7 (10 years/150,000 miles). Updated pistons with improved ring design are used in the repair. Use 0W-20 synthetic oil and check level every 1,000 miles.

Use 0W-20 synthetic oil and check level every 1,000 miles.

rows.title: Valve Cover Gasket Oil Leak
rows.howToFix: Replace valve cover gaskets and spark plug tube seals. For the V6, both front and rear valve covers should be done together. Use genuine Toyota gaskets for best sealing. Clean the valve cover and cylinder head mating surfaces thoroughly before installing new gaskets. The I4 is a straightforward 1-2 hour job. The V6 rear cover is 3-4 hours due to access difficulty.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Water Pump Leak (2GR-FE V6)
rows.howToFix: Replace water pump (Aisin WPT-190 or Toyota 16100-09515). Replace thermostat and serpentine belt at the same time. Use Toyota SLLC coolant. The job is moderately accessible on the V6 Venza with 2-3 hours shop labor.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Hybrid Fuel Tank Underfills and Inaccurate Fuel Gauge
rows.howToFix: Toyota attributes part of the shortfall to an undocumented hybrid fuel reserve and advises refueling below ~1/4 tank so the gauge calibrates. Where the gauge or fill is clearly defective, dealers have replaced fuel tank/sender assemblies under the support program used for the RAV4 Hybrid. A separate program (W63) addresses high-pressure fuel pump leakage/odor on some units.

rows.title: Hybrid System Inverter and 12V Battery Issues
rows.howToFix: Replace 12V auxiliary battery with AGM type (Toyota recommends their TrueStart battery). Install a battery tender/maintainer if the vehicle sits for extended periods. For hybrid system errors, dealer software update addresses most communication faults. Ensure the 12V battery terminals are clean and tight.

rows.title: Exhaust Heat Shield Rattle
rows.howToFix: Identify the loose heat shield by carefully pressing on each shield with the engine running (be careful of hot exhaust components). Re-secure with large hose clamps ($3-$5 each) around the heat shield and exhaust pipe. Dealers may spot-weld the shield back in place under warranty. As a last resort, the heat shield can be removed, though this is not recommended as it protects underbody components from exhaust heat.
rows.dispositionReason: No positive owner-buyable repair prescription was found.

rows.title: Infotainment Reboots / Goes Blank (TSB T-SB-0055-22)
rows.howToFix: Per TSB T-SB-0055-22, the dealer replaces the Integration Control Module (840C0-48020), covered under the 36-month/36,000-mile basic warranty when the condition occurs. A soft reset (hold the power/volume knob ~10 seconds) can clear temporary glitches but is not a permanent fix. Any replacement display must be VIN-synchronized with Techstream.
rows.dispositionReason: At least one replacement is conditional on a stated diagnostic result.

rows.title: Rear Turn Signal Failure from Water Intrusion (Recall 22V033)
rows.howToFix: Under recall 22V033 (Toyota 22TA01), dealers replace both rear turn-signal LED bulbs with improved units and, if needed, the rear turn-signal lamp assembly, free of charge. Owners can verify their VIN at nhtsa.gov or call Toyota at 800-331-4331.

rows.title: Spontaneous Windshield Cracking and Chipping
rows.howToFix: No recall exists; replacement is the only fix at roughly $1,000-$1,600, more if the Toyota Safety Sense forward camera requires recalibration. Owners use comprehensive insurance glass coverage and may join the class action. Dealers should recalibrate the forward camera after any windshield replacement.
rows.dispositionReason: The prescribed remedy is dealer, campaign, recall, or software work.

rows.title: Star Gaze Fixed Panoramic Roof Spontaneous Cracking and Burn/Spark Marks
rows.howToFix: Toyota generally does not cover crack-only cases under the new-vehicle warranty without a documented manufacturing defect; owners are advised to file a Dealer Problem Report (DPR) and use comprehensive insurance glass coverage. Burn/spark and electrochromic frost-feature failures have led Toyota to replace the glass roof assembly under warranty in some documented cases.
rows.dispositionReason: No positive owner-buyable repair prescription was found.

rows.title: Vehicle Stability Control Fails to Re-Enable on Restart (Recall 22V239)
rows.howToFix: Under recall 22V239 (Toyota 22TA03, Lexus 22LA01), dealers reprogram/update the Skid Control ECU software free of charge so VSC defaults to 'On' at each restart. Owner letters were mailed May 27, 2022; owners can confirm at nhtsa.gov or call Toyota at 800-331-4331.

rows.title: Interior Door Handle Breaking
rows.howToFix: Replace the interior door handle assembly (Toyota 69205-52080 for left front, 69206-52060 for right front). Aftermarket replacements are available for $15-30. This is a simple DIY repair requiring door panel removal. Replace all handles at the same time since they all use the same brittle plastic.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Exterior Door Handle Breakage
rows.howToFix: Replace the broken door handle assembly ($30-$80 for aftermarket, $80-$120 OEM). The replacement requires removing the inner door panel and disconnecting the latch rod. Some owners apply a small amount of silicone lubricant to the handle mechanism to prevent stiff operation in cold weather that leads to breakage. Always pull the handle gently in freezing conditions.
rows.dispositionReason: The solution prescribes an owner-buyable component or existing commerce requires re-review.

rows.title: Front Engine Mount Premature Failure
rows.howToFix: Replace the front engine mount (Toyota part 12361-21080 or equivalent). The repair is straightforward — support the engine from below, remove the through-bolt and bracket, and install the new mount. OEM mount costs $60-$100, aftermarket $30-$50. Replace all three mounts if the vehicle has over 120,000 miles, as the others are likely worn too.
rows.dispositionReason: At least one replacement is conditional on a stated diagnostic result.

rows.title: Electric Power Steering (EPS) Failure
rows.howToFix: Diagnose with Toyota Techstream to determine if the EPS motor or control module has failed. Replace EPS motor assembly (Toyota 45250-52210) or EPS ECU. Used EPS columns from salvage yards ($200-400) are a cost-effective option. After replacement, perform EPS calibration/initialization with Techstream.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: Diagnose with Toyota Techstream to determine if the EPS motor or control module has failed.

rows.title: 4-Speed Automatic Transmission Shudder and Harsh Shifts
rows.howToFix: Perform triple drain-and-fill with Toyota WS ATF (or Toyota Type T-IV for older models). If shudder persists, torque converter replacement. Regular ATF changes every 30,000 miles prevent the issue. The 4-speed automatic is otherwise quite reliable when maintained.
rows.dispositionReason: At least one replacement is conditional on a stated diagnostic result.
